The problem is the weird mix of metrics and numbers that only hold at a statistical population-wide level, and ones that are true on the individual level. Even in this article, they go from talking about BMI and associated risk, which is a perfectly valid statistical metric but not very useful as a personal metric, to talking about individual risk. Yes, an individual's BMI does dictate their statistical risk of health problems, but that's analogous to saying that teenagers are more likely to get into car crashes. Which (I assume) is correct, but that doesn't mean that an individual teenager is more likely to get in a car crash than another individual adult. If the adult is an aggressive driver, whereas the teenager is a very defensive one, the teen is still less likely to be in a car crash.

That's why you get movements like HAAS, who misinterpret some statistical study or tool and use it to justify individual health and fitness.

And then on the flip side, you get people like this kind individual I had a discussion with earlier, who also misinterpret the data and tools to say that, since statistically someone who matches certain metrics is statistically more likely to develop certain health issues, every individual who matches those metrics is affected by these health risks, which goes back to the teenagers and car crashes analogy.

tl;dr: Statistics is non-trivial and BMI is not gospel.

Everything in healthcare where you talk about risk factors and chance of disease is all about Bayes' theorem. We can talk about populations and say that having a BMI of X increases the percentage of people who will get diabetes by Y amount.

However on the individual patient level it's harder to suss out. When I talk to my patients about risk the single best way to explain things is with NNT and NNH. NNT is the number of people you need to treat with a specific problem or risk factor to prevent a single bad event. So say with people who are having a heart attack, you must give 42 people an aspirin to prevent one death. That BTW is considered a good NNT, especially since the NNH (number needed to harm) is about 350 (moderate to severe bleeding). It's considered so important that CMS measures hospital quality and determines how much hospitals get paid based on what percentage of heart attack patients get an aspirin within 30 minutes of arrival.

So what is the NNT to prevent one significant cardiac event by using weight loss surgery is about 50. Now the thing is, bariatric surgery is the single most effective treatment for obesity that we have (comparing to nutritionist, medications, support groups, and even inpatient treatment.) So the NNT for those interventions are substantially higher - each is over 100, and thus getting into the shitty range.

So when I treat patients with negative health behaviors (diet/activity/obesity, smoking, drug use, alcohol abuse, whatever) I frame it using one of the mantras of the HAES movement which is asking what can we do to improve health while meeting the patient where they are. This is all classic stages of change motivational interviewing. If I meet someone who isn't even contemplating a change with demands that they comply with a program to address their obesity, addiction to tobacco/alcohol/drugs, high risk sexual behavior, I may as well be talking to a brick wall.

There is a rare person who responds to being called a fat pig or a filthy addict, but most people won't and you're an idiot if you try it.
